messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Depression scores on the HADs improved significantly more with vitamin D3 than with placebo in IBS-D patients.
Sentence: "Symptoms severity, QoL, HADs-depression, and VSI score improved significantly in the vitamin D group as compared to the placebo group (P-values: <0.001, 0.049, 0.023, and 0.008; respectively)."
Measured as: HADs-depression score
Population: Adults aged 18-65 with diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome
Intervention: Vitamin D3 50,000 IU/week for 9 weeks
Comparator: Placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 74
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: No consistent interaction between vitamin D treatment and baseline CRP on depressive symptoms across outcomes.
Sentence: "No consistent interaction between treatment and baseline CRP was observed across outcomes."
Measured as: depressive symptoms (BDI-II, DISYPS, self- and proxy-rated)
Population: Depressed, vitamin D-deficient adolescents (25(OH)D ≤ 30 nmol/l, BDI-II ≥ 14)
Intervention: Vitamin D 2640 IU/day for 28 days plus treatment as usual
Comparator: Placebo plus treatment as usual
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 92
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

content.text: {"rationale":"Study A tests vitamin D3 against placebo on depression scores, while Study B's null concerns a treatment-by-baseline-CRP interaction rather than a main effect, so the two findings do not measure the same thing despite the shared outcome.","verdict":"apparent","reason":"outcome_measure","also_differs":["population","intervention"],"detail":"Study B's null is a treatment x baseline CRP interaction, not the overall vitamin D effect on depressive symptoms, so it does not conflict with Study A's main effect"}
